title: Draft Memorandum of Conversation of a Meeting Held in New York, November 16, 1952  The source text did not indicate the drafter, security classification, or date of the memorandum. From the context, it was probably a transcription of the actual discussion put in the third person. Acheson describes this meeting in his Present at the Creation, p. 701, thus: “At my request Secretary Lovett and General Bradley came to New York on November 16 for a meeting with them [the British and Pearson]. My purpose was to get away from talk about what would influence the Chinese Communists toward an armistice and to have those responsible for the Eighth Army state clearly the dangers in the field that Menon’s loose plan for dealing with the prisoners would present. My colleagues did their best but the meeting was too large; the talk wandered and did not have the effect I hoped for.” An unsigned three-page memorandum of conversation dated Nov. 17, 1952, prepared by Lt. Col. Jack B. Matthews from notes he had taken at the meeting on Nov. 16 in New York, is in General Bradley’s file, 091 Korea, 1952, National Archives Record Group 218. Also present at the meeting were Jeffery Kitchen, Assistant to the Secretary of State; A.A. Duff, Private Secretary to Selwyn Lloyd; S.F. Rae of the Canadian Department of External Affairs; and Lieutenant Colonel Matthews of G–3, Department of the Army.

title: Resolution 610 (VII), Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly, December 3, 1952  Source: Reprinted from American Foreign Policy, 1950–1955: Basic Documents, vol. II, pp. 2651–2654. In the plenary session of the General Assembly on Dec. 3, the revised Indian draft was adopted by an overwhelming majority. The final version was identical with that approved in the First Committee, with one exception: an amendment adopted by a separate vote which added the phrase “so that an immediate cease-fire would result and be effected” in the paragraph requesting the President of the Assembly to communicate the proposals to the People’s Republic of China and to North Korea. The Soviet representative submitted to the Assembly amendments and a draft resolution identical to those he submitted in the First Committee, but they were rejected by the Assembly by large margins. For a report of the session, see UN document A/PV.399.
